Claude loads either tool when it needs it, and if one appears only as a deferred tool's name, Claude loads it the way this session loads deferred tools before calling it.

**Claude never publishes** a page that impersonates a real person or organization, for example by using their name, branding, byline or domain. Claude also never publishes fabricated records, receipts or reviews presented as genuine, forms or flows that collect credentials or payment details under false pretenses, or content that targets a private individual. Claude refuses whether it wrote the page or the person supplied it, and whatever purpose is claimed, such as a prop or a test, when the page would work as the real thing. If publishing is refused, Claude does not suggest other ways to host or share the page.

action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

edits.description: publish: small changes Claude makes to the file at `file_path` in this same call, instead of editing the file with Edit and publishing after. Use it on a page (add `url` to update an artifact from another conversation) or on one data file of an artifact made from a type (its `url`, with that file as `file_path`). Not allowed with `type_url` or `files`. Each old_str is text copied exactly from the file as it now stands and must occur in it exactly once; new_str takes its place (empty deletes it). The edits apply in order, all or none: the file is published with them and then saved with them on disk, so it stays the source for later changes; on a miss nothing is changed or published, and the result says which edit failed and why.

old_str.description: Text copied exactly from the file; must occur once.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (a dashboard that shows data, anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

schema.name: ScheduleWakeup
schema.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

1	# Issue #230: a web control surface on the remote port. Investigation notes
2	
3	Worktree: `/Users/sbgragent/.dispatch/worktrees/50e56c62`, HEAD `7fe8949` (Release 0.4.1).
4	Scope: read only. Nothing built, run, or changed in the tree. Browser and platform behaviour is not verified here; every such claim is an open question below.
5	
6	Read: `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/design.md` (trust boundary; remote status), `docs/lessons.md`, `docs/remote-client.md` §0–5 and §10–13 (§6–9 not read in full), `src/adapters/remote.rs`, `src/app.rs` (`serve_remote` and the remote handlers), `src/ui/remote.rs`, `src/core/remote.rs`, `src/ports/remote.rs`, `control/src/lib.rs` (`SessionView`), `src/ui/cards.rs` (excerpt), the Swift text pairing path, and the `tests/remote.rs` HTTP helper.
7	
8	---
9	
10	## 1. Code the issue touches
11	
12	### Transport (`src/adapters/remote.rs`)
13	
14	- **:530–552 `respond()`**: the only response writer. It hard-codes `Content-Type: application/json` (line 545) and `Connection: keep-alive`. It takes a status and a body, with no way to add headers.
15	- **:389–393 `RemoteReply`**: `status`, `body`, `authenticated`. No headers field.
16	- **:444–514 `read_request`**: keeps method, path, query, body, `bearer` (from `Authorization` only, :487–490) and the WebSocket key (:491–494). It does not keep cookies, `Host`, `Origin`, `User-Agent` or `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`.
17	- **:519–526 `respond_upgrade`**: writes the 101 with no subprotocol echo.
18	- **:770–867 `connection()`**: per connection. The path rate limit runs first (:788–795). Then the request goes to the frame over a 64-deep channel, and a full channel answers 503 (:810–825). The answer waits up to 60 s (:827). The connection moves to the paired pool on an authenticated reply (:835–849), and the reply is written at :864.
19	- **:567–568, :701–707**: pools of 4 unauthenticated and 12 paired. A socket is counted as unauthenticated at accept (:707). It moves to the paired pool only on an authenticated reply. A keep-alive socket that never authenticates holds its slot until it closes or its idle timeout (`IDLE_TIMEOUT`, :573, 30 s) expires.
20	- **:623–639 `Limits`**: only `/api/v1/pair` and `/api/v1/info` are rate-limited. Every other path is unlimited.
21	- **:95–128 `make_identity`**: `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())`. The certificate has no subjectAltName, only a CN of `Switchboard <uuid>`. Its validity is rcgen's default (the doc comment says "never expires in practice").
22	- **:144–155 `tls_config`**: no ALPN is set.
23	- **:168–180 `pinned_client`**: the native client's SPKI verifier.
24	- **tests/remote.rs:245–298 `http()`**: the test client. It parses only `Content-Length` from the response, sends `Host: localhost`, and sends only an `Authorization` bearer. It cannot read `Set-Cookie`, `Content-Type` or any security header.
25	
26	### Host dispatch (`src/app.rs`)
27	
28	- **:3017–3123 `serve_remote`**: runs on the frame.
29	  - :3023–3025: any path without the `/api/v1/` prefix is refused with 404 through `refuse`. So `GET /` is a frame request today and gets a 404.
30	  - :3028 `info` and :3029 `pair` are served before authentication.
31	  - :3032 `authenticate`, then :3036 the `events` upgrade.
32	  - :3044–3117 the allowlist match, with a catch-all refusal at :3108–3116.
33	  - :3119 hides worker records unless `scope=all`.
34	- **:3127–3152 `authenticate`**: a bearer only. It returns 401 "pair this device first" with no bearer, and 401 "the token is not known; pair again" for an unknown or revoked token (:3142–3148). It also calls `DeviceSeen`.
35	- **:3159–3175 `remote_command`**: checks control scope (403 `scope`), then reads the body's `op`.
36	- **:2723–2762 `remote_subscribe`**: requires an upgrade. It queues `hello`, registers the subscriber, and returns `authenticated: true`.
37	- **:3568–3599 `remote_info`**: capabilities at :3580 (`read, control, draft, scope, tickets, evidence, create`). It has no field describing the caller, so no device can learn its own scope or name from it.
38	- **:3606–3673 `remote_pair`**: checks the SPKI (:3636) before the code (:3646). It creates the device with the window's scope, returns `{token, scope, server_id, device_id}` in an envelope with `authenticated: false` (:3672), and dispatches `Paired`, which closes the window.
39	- **:3730–3741 `envelope`**: `{epoch, revision, body}`.
40	- **:3754–3770 `refuse`**: logs method and path only (:3762–3766). A query string is therefore not logged by refusals.
41	- **:3662** is the only place `scope` is returned to a device (in the pair reply).
42	
43	### Core and state
44	
45	- **`src/core/remote.rs`**: the `OpenPairing`, `ClosePairing`, `PairingFailed`, `Paired`, `RevokeDevice` and `SetDeviceScope` arms. `new_device` trims the name to 64 characters and takes the scope from the window.
46	- **`src/core/action.rs:972–973`**: `PAIRING_WINDOW` is 5 minutes and `PAIRING_ATTEMPTS` is 3. The pairing window is in memory only, per the doc comment at :290.
47	- **`src/ports/remote.rs:96–107` `PairedDevice`**: `id`, `name`, `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen` (serde default). It has no schema field and no kind field.
48	- **`src/app.rs` ~2783–2840**: startup. A missing key makes a new identity and clears the devices (the design doc says so too).
49	
50	### Pairing window (`src/ui/remote.rs`)
51	
52	- **:155–166**: the QR payload is JSON `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`.
53	- **:157–159**: `addresses` holds one entry, `local_address()` plus the port.
54	- **:172 and :280–299**: the QR texture.
55	- **:199–206 "Copy invite"**: copies the JSON.
56	- **:70–76**: the redaction sentence in the dialog.
57	- **:110–113**: the "Allow devices on the local network" checkbox (`listen.lan`, off by default).
58	- **:214–224**: scope radio, Read by default. **:230–276**: device rows with scope, last seen, and Revoke.
59	
60	### Wire view and card excerpt
61	
62	- **`control/src/lib.rs:637` `SessionView`**: `card` (a string), `waiting`, `waiting_reason`, `trust_question`, `kind`, `resume_id`, `last_stop_at_ms`, `quiet_secs`, `last_activity_ms`, `transcript`. **It has no excerpt field.**
63	- **`src/ui/cards.rs:176–178` and `:558–575`**: an agent card's excerpt is computed in the UI from the transcript's last turn (first line of the final text, else the last activity, else the prompt), clamped to 160 characters.
64	
65	### Native text path
66	
67	- **`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift`**: the usage text and the `pair` case. One argument goes to `PairingInvite.parse`; three arguments are host, code and SPKI.
68	- **`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift`**, end of file: `PairingInvite` decodes JSON only (`Wire.decode`). `KeyFingerprint.short` is the owner-comparison form.
69	
70	### Docs and other
71	
72	- **`docs/remote-client.md`**: §4.1 bounds (:124–131); §4.3 endpoint table (:157–192) and the allowlist sentence (:194); §5 pairing (:302–319; the QR JSON at :309; "never in a URL" at :312); §10 status (:429–469); §11 tests (:471–510).
73	- **`docs/design.md`**: the trust-boundary paragraph (about :240–256); the remote client status (:3107 on).
74	- **`README.md:267`**: `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT`. The Layout table and dev-aid list need entries for any `web/` file.
75	- **`docs/lessons.md:27–29`** ("Keep `ui.rs` dumb") and CLAUDE.md's rule that logic under `src/ui/` moves to the core. The planned page reconciles revisions in JavaScript; §4.4 of the spec puts that in the client.
76	- No `web/` directory exists.
77	
78	---
79	
80	## 2. The on-disk record and its rehydration, before the pane
81	
82	**Host, today.**
83	- `identity.json`: `server_id`, `server_name`, the certificate (DER, base64), `spki_sha256`, `created`, `listen {lan, port}`. The private key is a Keychain item, `remote-key:<server_id>`. Startup restores these through `IdentityLoaded`.
84	- `devices.json`: the list of `PairedDevice`. A browser pairing adds one record like any other. Its `name` is whatever `device_name` the body carries, trimmed to 64 characters. Its scope is the window's scope. The host stores only `token_sha256`.
85	- Restart: `IdentityLoaded` restores the devices. `device_by_token` matches the hash. A browser that still holds its token therefore works again after a relaunch, provided the identity and its Keychain key survive.
86	- Keychain lost (or an unsigned rebuild, per CLAUDE.md): a new identity is made, the devices are cleared, and every token gets 401. The browser's certificate trust also breaks, since the certificate changes.
87	- Pairing window: in memory, gone on relaunch. Nothing to rehydrate.
88	- The page's assets are compiled in. They are not records.
89	
90	**Browser, per the issue (none exists yet).** The token (cookie or page memory, decision 2). The pinned key from the URL, if the plan keeps it, and where. The browser's own certificate exception for the host's address and port.
91	
92	**Session data is not new.** Projects, sessions and their state come from the existing records (`SessionRecord`, `views.json`) through the read models the headset already uses. The page's view state is in memory only.
93	
94	**The pane, after that record.** The page loads `GET /`, which is a new static route. The script reads `code`, `key` and `id` from the query and calls `history.replaceState`. It then calls `GET /api/v1/info`, compares the key, and calls `POST /api/v1/pair` with `{code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. The reply's token is kept. Then the page calls `GET /api/v1/projects`, `GET /api/v1/waiting` and `GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/sessions` and renders groups, waiting ones first, marked from `waiting` and `waiting_reason`. It opens `/api/v1/events` with the token, applies `hello`, snapshots, and refetches on `changed`.
95	
96	Three gaps show in that pane:
97	- The card's one-line excerpt is not on the wire.
98	- The device's scope is not readable after pairing, so the reply box cannot be hidden on reload.
99	- The session screen or last response is a separate request per session.
100	
101	---
102	
103	## 3. Findings from the tree
104	
105	1. **Static responses need a writer that can set headers.** `respond()` is the only writer and hard-codes JSON; `RemoteReply` has no headers. The CSP, `Cache-Control`, `Referrer-Policy`, `Content-Type` and any `Set-Cookie` all need one. Every construction site of `RemoteReply` (in `app.rs` and tests; I did not count them) changes if the struct gains a field.
106	2. **Static assets can skip the frame.** Constant bytes need no core state. Answering them on the connection thread matches §4.1's rule that content work stays off the frame. On the frame, each page load costs drain slots (8 per pass) and channel depth, and a page load is several requests.
107	3. **The unauthenticated pool counts sockets, not requests.** A browser loading one page can open several sockets to one origin. Each one not yet carrying a bearer holds one of four slots from accept until it authenticates or times out. The pairing POST, or a new socket from the paired device, can therefore be closed at accept (:701–706). The socket count browsers use is [source]; the effect is [run].
108	4. **Token transport needs parser changes.** `read_request` reads only `Authorization`. A cookie needs cookie parsing. A subprotocol token needs parsing and an echo in `respond_upgrade` (:519–526), which the browser requires when it offers a subprotocol [source].
109	5. **Cookies are ambient, and nothing checks `Origin`.** `read_request` drops `Origin`. Today's bearer design is safe because browsers never attach `Authorization` on their own. Cookie-authenticated state changes (`send`, `resume`, `trust`, new session, drafts, dictation, ticket commands) and the `events` upgrade would ride along on any same-site request. Whether `SameSite=Strict` stops that depends on [source] questions below.
110	6. **No `Host` check.** `read_request` ignores `Host`. That matters for DNS rebinding against unauthenticated reads (`/info`, `/pair`) [source].
111	7. **The certificate has no SAN.** A browser checks the name and the validity period, not only the key. A click-through therefore accepts a warning with more than one cause, and the SPKI check the issue relies on is the native client's, not the browser's. Browser behaviour is [source].
112	8. **Cookies are not port-scoped.** Two instances on one machine at one address, on different ports (the `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT` dev aid, README:267), would share a cookie name and overwrite each other's token. Name the cookie per `server_id` if one is used; the page can learn `server_id` from `/info`. [source] for the scoping rule.
113	9. **No endpoint tells a device its scope or name after pairing.** `scope` is returned only by `/pair` (:3662). `/info` is unauthenticated and has no caller field (:3568–3599). The issue's "device's scope in the header" and its "hide the reply box" need a new read, which the issue allows only when the page cannot do without one.
114	10. **The card's excerpt is not on the wire.** `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637`) has no excerpt, and §4.3 names a `last_message` on the Stop hook that the tree does not have. Today the UI derives the excerpt from the transcript (`cards.rs:558`). The page would need a new additive field or a second request per card.
115	11. **The QR carries one address.** `addresses` has one entry (`ui/remote.rs:157–164`), so the URL does too. The native path decodes JSON only (`Info.swift`, `PairingInvite.parse`), and the CLI's one-argument form assumes JSON. "Copy invite" copies JSON (`ui/remote.rs:199–206`). A URL changes that text and both native parsers unless one keeps JSON.
116	12. **The code reaches the host in a request line, and the page's own requests may leak it.** `refuse` logs path only, so no refusal logs the code. The static route must keep that rule. The page's script and CSS are same-origin subresources loaded while the URL still holds the query. Under the default referrer policy, same-origin requests carry the full URL in `Referer` [source]. A `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` header on the page is needed.
117	13. **Browser history keeps the URL.** Navigation records the URL with its query in the browser's history, which `replaceState` does not rewrite [source]. The code is single-use and is spent by the first `/pair`, and the window closes after 5 minutes (`action.rs:972`). The residual exposure is a history entry for a spent code.
118	14. **The browser-side key check protects little.** The URL's key is genuine (it came from the host's screen). But the script and `/info` come from whoever answers the connection. An impostor serving its own page answers `/info` with whatever key it likes. This matches the issue's own caveat; nothing in the tree gives the browser a pin.
119	15. **The allowlist and the pairing rule change.** §5 says nothing but `/info` and `/pair` is served before pairing, and §4.3 says the allowlist is explicit. The static paths need a new explicit set, checked before `serve_remote`'s prefix test (:3023) or on the connection thread.
120	16. **Test helpers limit what can be tested.** `http()` (tests/remote.rs:245–298) reads no headers but `Content-Length`, so header assertions need the helper extended. `call()` runs requests on the test thread through the frame, and a connection-thread route has no frame hook. Existing pairing tests: `a_pairing_inside_the_window_gives_a_token…` (:477), `a_wrong_pin_fails_at_the_handshake…` (:1395), `pair_is_rate_limited_per_listener` (:1405), `the_allowlist_refuses_everything_else…` (:681). The client fixtures (27 JSON files in `client/Fixtures`) and `the_client_fixtures_decode_on_both_sides` (:1828) cover Swift and CLI shapes, not HTML or a fourth consumer.
121	17. **`PairedDevice` has no version or kind field** (`ports/remote.rs:96–107`). CLAUDE.md's `SCHEMA_VERSION` rule covers `model.rs`; `ports/remote.rs` types are outside it. `last_seen` is a precedent for a `#[serde(default)]` addition.
122	18. **The page reconciles revisions in JavaScript.** §4.4 puts that in the client, which is right for the native client. CLAUDE.md and `lessons.md` want logic in the core, not in UI code. The page is not under `src/ui/`, but the spirit applies.
123	
124	---
125	
126	## 4. What I did not check
127	
128	- I did not build, run, or test anything. No `cargo test`, no live app, no `curl`, no browser.
129	- I read `tests/remote.rs` only at the helper and at test names. I did not read any test body or any fixture's contents.
130	- I did not read `remote_content_route` (:1947), `remote_draft`, `remote_dictation`, or the ticket handlers, beyond their signatures.
131	- I did not read `docs/remote-client.md` §6–9, the rest of the `design.md` remote status, or the visionOS app sources.
132	- I did not read the Swift `ConnectionManager`, `HostClient`, or the visionOS paste path, so the "headset pairs from Bonjour and a typed code" claim is not checked here.
133	- I did not count `RemoteReply` construction sites, and did not confirm how `devices.json` is serialized (whether it is a bare array).
134	- I did not check whether `tungstenite` 0.30 can write a subprotocol echo through `respond_upgrade`; the upgrade is written by hand.
135	- I did not check `scripts/bundle.sh` or the Keychain ACL behaviour on a rebuilt bundle.
136	
137	---
138	
139	## Open questions
140	
141	- [source] Does Safari on iPhone or iPad, and Chrome on Android, let the owner proceed past a self-signed certificate that has no subjectAltName and only a CN, and does that exception persist per host, per host and port, or per session?
142	- [source] Does a proceeded-past certificate exception also apply to `wss://` on the same origin, and to `fetch`?
143	- [source] Does a browser refuse a self-signed leaf certificate whose validity runs to the rcgen default (year 4096; `adapters/remote.rs:95–100`), and does the answer differ when the owner clicks through?
144	- [owner] Decision 1: is the click-through the trust step (disclosed in the paired-devices dialog), or does the host offer its certificate for download and the owner installs it on the device first (which means a device to test the install on)?
145	- [owner] Is a click-through warning acceptable on the owner's own LAN for a surface that can send prompts to agents?
146	- [tree] If the certificate gains a SAN for the LAN address, does the spec treat that as a reissue over the same key (no rotation, since §5 pins the SPKI) or as a new identity? The tree has no reissue path; `identity.json` is written once (`docs/remote-client.md` §3.1).
147	- [source] Does `fetch` send a `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookie on same-origin requests and on the `wss://` handshake, under a click-through certificate?
148	- [source] Does a cookie set by `192.168.x.x:43187` reach the same address on another port? RFC 6265 §8.5 says cookies are not port-isolated; confirm the browser implementations.
149	- [source] Does SameSite treat a page on another port of the same IP, or on `localhost`, as same-site, so that `Strict` cookies still ride along? This decides whether an `Origin` check or a custom request header is needed.
150	- [source] Does a cross-origin WebSocket handshake carry `SameSite=Strict` cookies, and does the browser send `Origin` on the upgrade so the host can check it?
151	- [source] Does a non-simple request header (for example `X-Switchboard: 1`) force a CORS preflight that the host's refusal of `OPTIONS` blocks, so a cross-origin page cannot send a state-changing POST?
152	- [source] When a browser offers a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value, must the 101 echo one of them or the handshake fails?
153	- [tree] Does any native client send `Authorization` such that a cookie branch in `authenticate` changes its behaviour? (The CLI and visionOS send bearers; `SwitchboardTransport` was not read.)
154	- [owner] Decision 2: is the cookie a session cookie (lost on browser close, so re-pair each time) or persistent, and for how long? The spec says tokens do not expire.
155	- [owner] Where the pinned key lives on the device: `localStorage`, a cookie, or nowhere. Without one, "identity changed" on a later visit can only show as the browser's own certificate warning.
156	- [tree] Is `localStorage` used for anything if the token is a cookie? §5 allows only per-viewer conveniences there.
157	- [owner] Decision 3: is the JSON invite still needed by the CLI, the headset, or anything else, or does the URL replace it everywhere?
158	- [tree] The headset's paste path and `SwitchboardClientCore` decode the invite; not read, so whether they can take a URL is unknown.
159	- [source] Does iOS Camera open an `https://` URL with an IP and a self-signed certificate straight into Safari, and does the warning then appear inside Safari, or does a banner need a tap first?
160	- [run] Does the QR stay scannable with the URL form (a 43-character key hash, an 8-character code, the address), and at what size? The current JSON form is not measured either.
161	- [tree] The exact static path set (`/`, the script, the stylesheet, any favicon). The tree shows only one prefix check (`app.rs:3023`) and no static route.

# Issue #230: a web control surface on the remote port. Investigation notes

Worktree: `/Users/sbgragent/.dispatch/worktrees/50e56c62`, HEAD `7fe8949` (Release 0.4.1).
Scope: read only. Nothing built, run, or changed in the tree. Browser and platform behaviour is not verified here; every such claim is an open question below.

Read: `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/design.md` (trust boundary; remote status), `docs/lessons.md`, `docs/remote-client.md` §0–5 and §10–13 (§6–9 not read in full), `src/adapters/remote.rs`, `src/app.rs` (`serve_remote` and the remote handlers), `src/ui/remote.rs`, `src/core/remote.rs`, `src/ports/remote.rs`, `control/src/lib.rs` (`SessionView`), `src/ui/cards.rs` (excerpt), the Swift text pairing path, and the `tests/remote.rs` HTTP helper.

---

## 1. Code the issue touches

### Transport (`src/adapters/remote.rs`)

- **:530–552 `respond()`**: the only response writer. It hard-codes `Content-Type: application/json` (line 545) and `Connection: keep-alive`. It takes a status and a body, with no way to add headers.
- **:389–393 `RemoteReply`**: `status`, `body`, `authenticated`. No headers field.
- **:444–514 `read_request`**: keeps method, path, query, body, `bearer` (from `Authorization` only, :487–490) and the WebSocket key (:491–494). It does not keep cookies, `Host`, `Origin`, `User-Agent` or `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`.
- **:519–526 `respond_upgrade`**: writes the 101 with no subprotocol echo.
- **:770–867 `connection()`**: per connection. The path rate limit runs first (:788–795). Then the request goes to the frame over a 64-deep channel, and a full channel answers 503 (:810–825). The answer waits up to 60 s (:827). The connection moves to the paired pool on an authenticated reply (:835–849), and the reply is written at :864.
- **:567–568, :701–707**: pools of 4 unauthenticated and 12 paired. A socket is counted as unauthenticated at accept (:707). It moves to the paired pool only on an authenticated reply. A keep-alive socket that never authenticates holds its slot until it closes or its idle timeout (`IDLE_TIMEOUT`, :573, 30 s) expires.
- **:623–639 `Limits`**: only `/api/v1/pair` and `/api/v1/info` are rate-limited. Every other path is unlimited.
- **:95–128 `make_identity`**: `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())`. The certificate has no subjectAltName, only a CN of `Switchboard <uuid>`. Its validity is rcgen's default (the doc comment says "never expires in practice").
- **:144–155 `tls_config`**: no ALPN is set.
- **:168–180 `pinned_client`**: the native client's SPKI verifier.
- **tests/remote.rs:245–298 `http()`**: the test client. It parses only `Content-Length` from the response, sends `Host: localhost`, and sends only an `Authorization` bearer. It cannot read `Set-Cookie`, `Content-Type` or any security header.

### Host dispatch (`src/app.rs`)

- **:3017–3123 `serve_remote`**: runs on the frame.
  - :3023–3025: any path without the `/api/v1/` prefix is refused with 404 through `refuse`. So `GET /` is a frame request today and gets a 404.
  - :3028 `info` and :3029 `pair` are served before authentication.
  - :3032 `authenticate`, then :3036 the `events` upgrade.
  - :3044–3117 the allowlist match, with a catch-all refusal at :3108–3116.
  - :3119 hides worker records unless `scope=all`.
- **:3127–3152 `authenticate`**: a bearer only. It returns 401 "pair this device first" with no bearer, and 401 "the token is not known; pair again" for an unknown or revoked token (:3142–3148). It also calls `DeviceSeen`.
- **:3159–3175 `remote_command`**: checks control scope (403 `scope`), then reads the body's `op`.
- **:2723–2762 `remote_subscribe`**: requires an upgrade. It queues `hello`, registers the subscriber, and returns `authenticated: true`.
- **:3568–3599 `remote_info`**: capabilities at :3580 (`read, control, draft, scope, tickets, evidence, create`). It has no field describing the caller, so no device can learn its own scope or name from it.
- **:3606–3673 `remote_pair`**: checks the SPKI (:3636) before the code (:3646). It creates the device with the window's scope, returns `{token, scope, server_id, device_id}` in an envelope with `authenticated: false` (:3672), and dispatches `Paired`, which closes the window.
- **:3730–3741 `envelope`**: `{epoch, revision, body}`.
- **:3754–3770 `refuse`**: logs method and path only (:3762–3766). A query string is therefore not logged by refusals.
- **:3662** is the only place `scope` is returned to a device (in the pair reply).

### Core and state

- **`src/core/remote.rs`**: the `OpenPairing`, `ClosePairing`, `PairingFailed`, `Paired`, `RevokeDevice` and `SetDeviceScope` arms. `new_device` trims the name to 64 characters and takes the scope from the window.
- **`src/core/action.rs:972–973`**: `PAIRING_WINDOW` is 5 minutes and `PAIRING_ATTEMPTS` is 3. The pairing window is in memory only, per the doc comment at :290.
- **`src/ports/remote.rs:96–107` `PairedDevice`**: `id`, `name`, `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen` (serde default). It has no schema field and no kind field.
- **`src/app.rs` ~2783–2840**: startup. A missing key makes a new identity and clears the devices (the design doc says so too).

### Pairing window (`src/ui/remote.rs`)

- **:155–166**: the QR payload is JSON `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`.
- **:157–159**: `addresses` holds one entry, `local_address()` plus the port.
- **:172 and :280–299**: the QR texture.
- **:199–206 "Copy invite"**: copies the JSON.
- **:70–76**: the redaction sentence in the dialog.
- **:110–113**: the "Allow devices on the local network" checkbox (`listen.lan`, off by default).
- **:214–224**: scope radio, Read by default. **:230–276**: device rows with scope, last seen, and Revoke.

### Wire view and card excerpt

- **`control/src/lib.rs:637` `SessionView`**: `card` (a string), `waiting`, `waiting_reason`, `trust_question`, `kind`, `resume_id`, `last_stop_at_ms`, `quiet_secs`, `last_activity_ms`, `transcript`. **It has no excerpt field.**
- **`src/ui/cards.rs:176–178` and `:558–575`**: an agent card's excerpt is computed in the UI from the transcript's last turn (first line of the final text, else the last activity, else the prompt), clamped to 160 characters.

### Native text path

- **`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift`**: the usage text and the `pair` case. One argument goes to `PairingInvite.parse`; three arguments are host, code and SPKI.
- **`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift`**, end of file: `PairingInvite` decodes JSON only (`Wire.decode`). `KeyFingerprint.short` is the owner-comparison form.

### Docs and other

- **`docs/remote-client.md`**: §4.1 bounds (:124–131); §4.3 endpoint table (:157–192) and the allowlist sentence (:194); §5 pairing (:302–319; the QR JSON at :309; "never in a URL" at :312); §10 status (:429–469); §11 tests (:471–510).
- **`docs/design.md`**: the trust-boundary paragraph (about :240–256); the remote client status (:3107 on).
- **`README.md:267`**: `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT`. The Layout table and dev-aid list need entries for any `web/` file.
- **`docs/lessons.md:27–29`** ("Keep `ui.rs` dumb") and CLAUDE.md's rule that logic under `src/ui/` moves to the core. The planned page reconciles revisions in JavaScript; §4.4 of the spec puts that in the client.
- No `web/` directory exists.

---

## 2. The on-disk record and its rehydration, before the pane

**Host, today.**
- `identity.json`: `server_id`, `server_name`, the certificate (DER, base64), `spki_sha256`, `created`, `listen {lan, port}`. The private key is a Keychain item, `remote-key:<server_id>`. Startup restores these through `IdentityLoaded`.
- `devices.json`: the list of `PairedDevice`. A browser pairing adds one record like any other. Its `name` is whatever `device_name` the body carries, trimmed to 64 characters. Its scope is the window's scope. The host stores only `token_sha256`.
- Restart: `IdentityLoaded` restores the devices. `device_by_token` matches the hash. A browser that still holds its token therefore works again after a relaunch, provided the identity and its Keychain key survive.
- Keychain lost (or an unsigned rebuild, per CLAUDE.md): a new identity is made, the devices are cleared, and every token gets 401. The browser's certificate trust also breaks, since the certificate changes.
- Pairing window: in memory, gone on relaunch. Nothing to rehydrate.
- The page's assets are compiled in. They are not records.

**Browser, per the issue (none exists yet).** The token (cookie or page memory, decision 2). The pinned key from the URL, if the plan keeps it, and where. The browser's own certificate exception for the host's address and port.

**Session data is not new.** Projects, sessions and their state come from the existing records (`SessionRecord`, `views.json`) through the read models the headset already uses. The page's view state is in memory only.

**The pane, after that record.** The page loads `GET /`, which is a new static route. The script reads `code`, `key` and `id` from the query and calls `history.replaceState`. It then calls `GET /api/v1/info`, compares the key, and calls `POST /api/v1/pair` with `{code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. The reply's token is kept. Then the page calls `GET /api/v1/projects`, `GET /api/v1/waiting` and `GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/sessions` and renders groups, waiting ones first, marked from `waiting` and `waiting_reason`. It opens `/api/v1/events` with the token, applies `hello`, snapshots, and refetches on `changed`.

Three gaps show in that pane:
- The card's one-line excerpt is not on the wire.
- The device's scope is not readable after pairing, so the reply box cannot be hidden on reload.
- The session screen or last response is a separate request per session.

---

## 3. Findings from the tree

1. **Static responses need a writer that can set headers.** `respond()` is the only writer and hard-codes JSON; `RemoteReply` has no headers. The CSP, `Cache-Control`, `Referrer-Policy`, `Content-Type` and any `Set-Cookie` all need one. Every construction site of `RemoteReply` (in `app.rs` and tests; I did not count them) changes if the struct gains a field.
2. **Static assets can skip the frame.** Constant bytes need no core state. Answering them on the connection thread matches §4.1's rule that content work stays off the frame. On the frame, each page load costs drain slots (8 per pass) and channel depth, and a page load is several requests.
3. **The unauthenticated pool counts sockets, not requests.** A browser loading one page can open several sockets to one origin. Each one not yet carrying a bearer holds one of four slots from accept until it authenticates or times out. The pairing POST, or a new socket from the paired device, can therefore be closed at accept (:701–706). The socket count browsers use is [source]; the effect is [run].
4. **Token transport needs parser changes.** `read_request` reads only `Authorization`. A cookie needs cookie parsing. A subprotocol token needs parsing and an echo in `respond_upgrade` (:519–526), which the browser requires when it offers a subprotocol [source].
5. **Cookies are ambient, and nothing checks `Origin`.** `read_request` drops `Origin`. Today's bearer design is safe because browsers never attach `Authorization` on their own. Cookie-authenticated state changes (`send`, `resume`, `trust`, new session, drafts, dictation, ticket commands) and the `events` upgrade would ride along on any same-site request. Whether `SameSite=Strict` stops that depends on [source] questions below.
6. **No `Host` check.** `read_request` ignores `Host`. That matters for DNS rebinding against unauthenticated reads (`/info`, `/pair`) [source].
7. **The certificate has no SAN.** A browser checks the name and the validity period, not only the key. A click-through therefore accepts a warning with more than one cause, and the SPKI check the issue relies on is the native client's, not the browser's. Browser behaviour is [source].
8. **Cookies are not port-scoped.** Two instances on one machine at one address, on different ports (the `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT` dev aid, README:267), would share a cookie name and overwrite each other's token. Name the cookie per `server_id` if one is used; the page can learn `server_id` from `/info`. [source] for the scoping rule.
9. **No endpoint tells a device its scope or name after pairing.** `scope` is returned only by `/pair` (:3662). `/info` is unauthenticated and has no caller field (:3568–3599). The issue's "device's scope in the header" and its "hide the reply box" need a new read, which the issue allows only when the page cannot do without one.
10. **The card's excerpt is not on the wire.** `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637`) has no excerpt, and §4.3 names a `last_message` on the Stop hook that the tree does not have. Today the UI derives the excerpt from the transcript (`cards.rs:558`). The page would need a new additive field or a second request per card.
11. **The QR carries one address.** `addresses` has one entry (`ui/remote.rs:157–164`), so the URL does too. The native path decodes JSON only (`Info.swift`, `PairingInvite.parse`), and the CLI's one-argument form assumes JSON. "Copy invite" copies JSON (`ui/remote.rs:199–206`). A URL changes that text and both native parsers unless one keeps JSON.
12. **The code reaches the host in a request line, and the page's own requests may leak it.** `refuse` logs path only, so no refusal logs the code. The static route must keep that rule. The page's script and CSS are same-origin subresources loaded while the URL still holds the query. Under the default referrer policy, same-origin requests carry the full URL in `Referer` [source]. A `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` header on the page is needed.
13. **Browser history keeps the URL.** Navigation records the URL with its query in the browser's history, which `replaceState` does not rewrite [source]. The code is single-use and is spent by the first `/pair`, and the window closes after 5 minutes (`action.rs:972`). The residual exposure is a history entry for a spent code.
14. **The browser-side key check protects little.** The URL's key is genuine (it came from the host's screen). But the script and `/info` come from whoever answers the connection. An impostor serving its own page answers `/info` with whatever key it likes. This matches the issue's own caveat; nothing in the tree gives the browser a pin.
15. **The allowlist and the pairing rule change.** §5 says nothing but `/info` and `/pair` is served before pairing, and §4.3 says the allowlist is explicit. The static paths need a new explicit set, checked before `serve_remote`'s prefix test (:3023) or on the connection thread.
16. **Test helpers limit what can be tested.** `http()` (tests/remote.rs:245–298) reads no headers but `Content-Length`, so header assertions need the helper extended. `call()` runs requests on the test thread through the frame, and a connection-thread route has no frame hook. Existing pairing tests: `a_pairing_inside_the_window_gives_a_token…` (:477), `a_wrong_pin_fails_at_the_handshake…` (:1395), `pair_is_rate_limited_per_listener` (:1405), `the_allowlist_refuses_everything_else…` (:681). The client fixtures (27 JSON files in `client/Fixtures`) and `the_client_fixtures_decode_on_both_sides` (:1828) cover Swift and CLI shapes, not HTML or a fourth consumer.
17. **`PairedDevice` has no version or kind field** (`ports/remote.rs:96–107`). CLAUDE.md's `SCHEMA_VERSION` rule covers `model.rs`; `ports/remote.rs` types are outside it. `last_seen` is a precedent for a `#[serde(default)]` addition.
18. **The page reconciles revisions in JavaScript.** §4.4 puts that in the client, which is right for the native client. CLAUDE.md and `lessons.md` want logic in the core, not in UI code. The page is not under `src/ui/`, but the spirit applies.

---

## 4. What I did not check

- I did not build, run, or test anything. No `cargo test`, no live app, no `curl`, no browser.
- I read `tests/remote.rs` only at the helper and at test names. I did not read any test body or any fixture's contents.
- I did not read `remote_content_route` (:1947), `remote_draft`, `remote_dictation`, or the ticket handlers, beyond their signatures.
- I did not read `docs/remote-client.md` §6–9, the rest of the `design.md` remote status, or the visionOS app sources.
- I did not read the Swift `ConnectionManager`, `HostClient`, or the visionOS paste path, so the "headset pairs from Bonjour and a typed code" claim is not checked here.
- I did not count `RemoteReply` construction sites, and did not confirm how `devices.json` is serialized (whether it is a bare array).
- I did not check whether `tungstenite` 0.30 can write a subprotocol echo through `respond_upgrade`; the upgrade is written by hand.
- I did not check `scripts/bundle.sh` or the Keychain ACL behaviour on a rebuilt bundle.

---

## Open questions

- [source] Does Safari on iPhone or iPad, and Chrome on Android, let the owner proceed past a self-signed certificate that has no subjectAltName and only a CN, and does that exception persist per host, per host and port, or per session?
- [source] Does a proceeded-past certificate exception also apply to `wss://` on the same origin, and to `fetch`?
- [source] Does a browser refuse a self-signed leaf certificate whose validity runs to the rcgen default (year 4096; `adapters/remote.rs:95–100`), and does the answer differ when the owner clicks through?

- [source] Does `navigator.userAgent` identify an iPad? Desktop-mode iPadOS reports as a Mac. The UA header is not kept by `read_request` today.

- [owner] Name wording in the dialog, and whether browser devices are listed differently from native ones.
- [tree] Scope for a browser device is the window's scope, Read by default. A device cannot learn its scope after pairing (finding 9). Which new read, if any, the plan adds (`GET /api/v1/device`, or a caller field on an existing read)?
- [tree] Revocation and "pair again" look the same to the page: both are the 401 at `app.rs:3142–3148`. Does the plan need a distinct error code, an additive change to `refuse`?
- [tree] "Identity changed, pair again": the host deletes devices only on key rotation (`app.rs` ~2802–2840). Nothing on the host detects a client's stored key. This is a client-side rule the page must implement, so the question is which pinned key it stores (see the storage question above).
- [owner] Should the page appear only when the LAN checkbox is on? With it off, the listener is loopback, and the phone cannot reach the page at all.
- [tree] Confirm that statics on the connection thread leave the frame's 4 ms budget (design §10) untouched, and that nothing else in `serve_remote` changes.
- [owner] Is a second instance on the same machine (the dev aid) a case the page must handle, or is the cookie name per `server_id` enough?
- [run] The acceptance flow end to end: a phone on the same LAN, the owner's click-through, a session moving to the top on `changed {waiting}`, a reply sent and seen, a revoke shown on the next request. Not run; needs a phone and a LAN.
- [owner] Restart-survives-a-browser-pairing needs a signed bundle (`scripts/bundle.sh`), since an unsigned rebuild loses the Keychain key and every pairing (CLAUDE.md, platform rules). That needs the owner's signing identity on this Mac.
- [source] The issue's own claims are not verified and are listed here as questions: a phone's camera opens a URL in the browser; `localStorage` is readable by any script on the origin while a cookie marked `HttpOnly` is not; browsers cannot pin an SPKI; a browser sends a cookie on the WebSocket handshake.
